summary: This informational RFC lists requirements for a tunnel-based EAP method. The method would use TLS to set up a secure tunnel that supports password authentication, EAP authentication, and the transport of additional data.

eli5.summary: You first put a secret tube between you and the server, then pass the password through it. This lists what the tube must do.

questions: what are the requirements for a tunnel eap method
what is an eap tunnel method
what is cryptographic binding in eap
why does eap need a tls tunnel
subtitle: The checklist a TLS-based EAP tunnel method had to meet: protect passwords, shield weak methods and hide who is logging in.

tldr.problem: Several EAP methods already wrapped authentication in a TLS tunnel (PEAP, EAP-TTLS, EAP-FAST), but a single method was wanted that covers password login, protection of weak EAP methods, identity privacy and extra data in a standard way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists use cases and then states MUST, SHOULD and MAY requirements for the TLS tunnel, the payload carried inside it, password authentication and inner EAP methods, including a cryptographic binding between the tunnel and the inner method.
tldr.outcome: It defines requirements, not a protocol. A candidate must support every use case marked MUST, and the Security Considerations warn about weak cipher suites, tunnel man-in-the-middle attacks and splitting the tunnel from the inner method.

today: RFC 6678 is an Informational RFC (July 2012), and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets requirements for a method rather than defining one.

sections.title: Why an EAP Tunnel Method
sections.content:
An EAP tunnel method is an EAP method that sets up a secure tunnel and then runs other EAP methods inside it. It can be used in any lower-layer protocol that supports EAP. Existing methods built on TLS include Protected EAP (PEAP), EAP-TTLS (RFC 5281) and EAP-FAST (RFC 4851). The RFC says this has generally worked well, so there is consensus to keep TLS as the basis.

Reasons to use a tunnel include protecting weak exchanges such as a username and password, hiding the peer's identity, chaining EAP methods, and carrying additional data. The document sets requirements for the tunnel method and for a password protocol that supports legacy password checks inside it. Its requirement words apply to the EAP Method Update (EMU) working group's method selection process.
sections.eli5: Imagine sending a secret note through a closed tube so nobody can peek. This memo says what a good tube must be like.

sections.title: Use Cases the Method Must Serve
sections.content:
The RFC gives nine use cases, and a candidate must support every one marked MUST.

  • Password authentication: transport a cleartext username and password to the EAP server without revealing it to anyone on the path. An attacker's advantage MUST come from interaction, not computation.
  • Protection of weak EAP methods: for example EAP-MD5 lacks mutual authentication and dictionary-attack protection. Cryptographic protection against tunnel man-in-the-middle attacks MUST be provided for all key-generating methods.
  • Chained EAP methods: for example authenticating both user and device, with protection against attacks on chaining.
  • Identity protection: the peer identity MUST NOT be obtainable by anyone but the EAP server that ends the tunnel, although a roaming peer may need to reveal the realm part of its outer identity.
  • Anonymous service access (SHOULD), Network Endpoint Assessment (SHOULD), client authentication during tunnel establishment (MUST), extensibility (MUST) and certificate-less authentication (MAY).

Where the tunnel has no server authentication, the inner method MUST resist dictionary attacks, cryptographic binding MUST be used, and the cipher suite MUST derive the master key from both client and server contributions, as ephemeral Diffie-Hellman suites do.
sections.eli5: The tube has to be useful in many situations: sending a password safely, helping weak locks stay safe, hiding your name, and checking that your device is healthy.

sections.title: Tunnel and TLS Requirements
sections.content:
The method MUST support TLS version 1.2 (RFC 5246) and may support earlier versions greater than SSL 2.0. It MUST NOT be tied to a single cryptographic algorithm and MUST allow run-time negotiation among an extensible set, so users can move on if an algorithm weakens.

For cipher suites, the method MUST give integrity-protected cipher suite negotiation, offer at least one mandatory-to-implement suite equivalent in strength to 128-bit AES, and provide certificate-based server authentication with optional certificate-based client authentication. Mandatory suites MUST NOT include mutually anonymous or static Diffie-Hellman suites.

Other tunnel requirements: message authentication must use a time-variant input for replay protection, the peer must not send its username or attributes in the clear, TLS session resumption MUST be supported, fragmentation and reassembly MUST be supported because messages can exceed one EAP message, and protocol version and type code outside the tunnel MUST be protected.
sections.eli5: The tube must be strong, must let both sides agree on a good lock, must be able to carry big messages in pieces, and must stop anyone from replaying an old message.

sections.title: Payload, Passwords and Inner Methods
sections.content:
Inside the tunnel, the payload MUST be extensible with attribute types and support the half-duplex request and response style of EAP. There MUST be a way to mark an attribute so the receiver reports if it does not understand it, vendor-specific attributes MUST be supported in separate namespaces, and separate result indications for intermediate and final results MUST be supported. Display strings from the server MUST be UTF-8.

For passwords, the cleartext exchange MUST be integrity and confidentiality protected, the server MUST be authenticated before the peer sends the password, the method MUST support checking certificate revocation (the SHOULD options are OCSP or SCVP), usernames and passwords in international languages MUST be supported, and password change MUST be supported.

For inner EAP methods, the tunnel MUST carry them without modification, MUST protect their negotiation from intermediaries and SHOULD support chaining them. Peer-initiated inner authentication and method metadata (such as user versus machine) are SHOULD requirements.
sections.eli5: Inside the tube, messages are like labeled cards that new kinds of cards can be added to. Passwords may only be handed over after you know who is at the other end.

sections.title: Cryptographic Binding
sections.content:
The tunnel method MUST bind the tunnel protocol to the inner EAP method. This cryptographic binding counters tunnel man-in-the-middle attacks, in which an attacker relays inner method messages to and from a peer that runs the method outside a tunnel or with an untrustworthy server. Binding prevents the attack completely without extra policy only if the inner method derives keys and is not vulnerable outside a tunnel. Weak or non-key-deriving inner methods still need security policies.

The usual approach mixes the tunnel key (TK) with the inner method key (MK) into a compound tunnel key (CTK), from which the EAP MSK, EMSK and transient keys are derived. For n sequential inner methods, a chained key CTK_i MUST be computed after each method, with CTK_0 equal to TK. Derived keys MUST have a lifetime no longer than any key above them in the hierarchy.
sections.eli5: Binding is like gluing the name tag on the tube itself, so nobody can swap the person inside after the tube is checked.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The tunnel is only as strong as its cipher suite. Anonymous Diffie-Hellman suites greatly increase risk, and a tunnel protocol that supports key establishment that can be broken on-line is prone to downgrading attacks. In mutually anonymous tunnels an adversary can set up one tunnel to the peer and another to the server and read everything, so the RFC requires server authentication.

In tunneled authentication, cryptographic binding thwarts tunnel man-in-the-middle attacks only if the inner method keys are strong enough. If the inner method gives no keys or weak keys, security policies MUST stop the peer from using the same credentials outside a protective tunnel or with an untrustworthy server.

Data outside the tunnel, such as the EAP type code or version numbers, MUST be protected if changing it can compromise the protocol. Ending the inner method at a different server than the tunnel needs care: for example, a cleartext password sent in a RADIUS password attribute gets only weak encryption, and a tunnel ended by another organization may not be trustworthy for the peer's secrets.
sections.eli5: A tube with a weak lock is nearly as bad as no tube. And if the tube ends at the wrong building, your secret can still leak on the way to the right one.

root.label: CTK
root.note: Compound tunnel key, derived from the tunnel key (TK) and the inner method key (MK)

children.label: TEK
children.note: Transient keys, such as encryption and integrity protection keys
